questions.question: A merchant in the port city of Lothal is exchanging bags of spices for copper ingots. He receives 15 ingots for every 2 bags of spices. If he brings 12 bags of spices to the market, how many copper ingots will he leave with?

solution.content: **Understand the exchange rate:** 2 bags of spices $=$ 15 copper ingots. So 1 bag of spices $= \frac{15}{2}$ ingots.
**Conclusion:** The merchant will leave with **90 copper ingots**.

questions.answer: The merchant will leave with **90 copper ingots**.

formulaBox.title: Unitary Method
formulaBox.content: $$\text{Value for } n \text{ items} = n \times \frac{\text{value for given items}}{\text{number of given items}}$$

questions.notes: **Exam Tip:** First find the value of one unit, then multiply by the required number of units.

questions.question: Look at the sequence of numbers on one column of the Ishango bone: 11, 13, 17, 19. What do these numbers have in common? List the next three numbers that fit this pattern.

solution.content: **Identify the common property:** The numbers 11, 13, 17 and 19 are all **prime numbers** — numbers that have exactly two factors: 1 and the number itself.
**Check each number:** 11 (factors 1, 11), 13 (factors 1, 13), 17 (factors 1, 17), 19 (factors 1, 19). None of them is divisible by any number other than 1 and itself.
**Find the next three primes after 19:** The next three prime numbers are **23, 29, 31**.

questions.answer: They are all **prime numbers**. The next three numbers are **23, 29, 31**.
questions.notes: **Historical note:** The Ishango bone (c. 20,000 BCE) contains tallies grouped as 11, 13, 17, 19 — the prime numbers between 10 and 20 — showing that the concept of numbers is tens of thousands of years old.

questions.question: We know that Natural Numbers are closed under addition (the sum of any two natural numbers is always a natural number). Are they closed under subtraction? Provide a couple of examples to justify your answer.

solution.content: **Recall the definition of closure:** A set is closed under an operation if performing that operation on any two members of the set always gives a result that is also in the set.
**Test subtraction with examples:** $5 - 3 = 2$ (a natural number ✓). But $3 - 5 = -2$ (a negative number, **not** a natural number ✗).

**Conclusion:** Since subtracting a larger natural number from a smaller one gives a negative number (or zero), the result is not always a natural number. Therefore, **natural numbers are NOT closed under subtraction**.

questions.answer: No, natural numbers are **not closed under subtraction**. Example: $3 - 5 = -2$, which is not a natural number.
questions.notes: **Common Mistake:** Students think closure means 'the operation works sometimes'. Closure requires the result to be in the set for ALL pairs. One counter-example is enough to disprove closure.

questions.question: Ancient Indians used the joints of their fingers to count, a practice still seen today. Each finger has 3 joints, and the thumb is used to count them. How many can you count on one hand? How does this relate to the ancient base-12 counting systems?

solution.content: **Count the joints:** Each finger (except the thumb) has 3 joints. The number of fingers used for counting is 4 (index, middle, ring, little).
**Total count on one hand:** $$4 \times 3 = 12$$ So one can count up to **12** on one hand using the thumb to point at each joint.

**Relation to base-12:** Since counting reaches 12 on one hand, this naturally leads to a **base-12 (duodecimal)** counting system. Ancient civilisations used base-12 for time (12 months, 12 hours), and it survives today in dozens (12 items) and inches (12 inches in a foot).

questions.answer: You can count up to **12** on one hand (4 fingers × 3 joints). This relates to the ancient **base-12 counting system**.
questions.notes: **Real-life connection:** Base-12 survives today in our language and units: a dozen = 12, 12 inches = 1 foot, 12 months = 1 year, and the clock uses 12 hours.
